{{short description|Concept in climate science}}
{{good article}}
{{use dmy dates|date=February 2020}}
[[File:Climate sensitivity diagram.svg|thumb|330x330px|Diagram of factors that determine climate sensitivity. After [[Carbon dioxide in Earth's atmosphere|increasing {{CO2}} levels]], there is an initial warming. This warming gets amplified by the net effect of [[Climate change feedbacks|climate feedbacks]]. ]]

'''Climate sensitivity''' is a key measure in [[climatology|climate science]] and describes how much Earth's surface will warm in response to a doubling of the [[Carbon dioxide in Earth's atmosphere|atmospheric carbon dioxide ({{CO2}}) concentration]].<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.metoffice.gov.uk/research/climate/understanding-climate/climate-sensitivity-explained|title=What is 'climate sensitivity'?|website=Met Office|language=en|access-date=2020-02-14|archive-date=7 May 2019|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190507124405/https://www.metoffice.gov.uk/research/climate/understanding-climate/climate-sensitivity-explained|url-status=live}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |title=Climate sensitivity: fact sheet |url=https://www.environment.gov.au/system/files/resources/d3a8654f-e1f1-4d3f-85a1-4c2d5f354047/files/factsheetclimatesensitivitycsiro-bureau.pdf |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200212201158/https://www.environment.gov.au/system/files/resources/d3a8654f-e1f1-4d3f-85a1-4c2d5f354047/files/factsheetclimatesensitivitycsiro-bureau.pdf |archive-date=12 February 2020 |access-date=12 February 2020 |publisher=Australian government. Department of the Environment.}}</ref> Its formal definition is: "The change in the surface temperature in response to a change in the atmospheric carbon dioxide (CO<sub>2</sub>) concentration or other radiative forcing."<ref name=":9">IPCC, 2021: [https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg1/downloads/report/IPCC_AR6_WGI_AnnexVII.pdf Annex VII: Glossary] [Matthews, J.B.R., V. Möller, R. van Diemen, J.S. Fuglestvedt, V. Masson-Delmotte, C.  Méndez, S. Semenov, A. Reisinger (eds.)]. In [https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg1/ Climate Change 2021: The Physical Science Basis. Contribution of Working Group I to the Sixth Assessment Report of the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change] [Masson-Delmotte, V., P. Zhai, A. Pirani, S.L. Connors, C. Péan, S. Berger, N. Caud, Y. Chen, L. Goldfarb, M.I. Gomis, M. Huang, K. Leitzell, E. Lonnoy, J.B.R. Matthews, T.K. Maycock, T. Waterfield, O. Yelekçi, R. Yu, and B. Zhou (eds.)]. Cambridge University Press, Cambridge, United Kingdom and New York, NY, USA, pp. 2215–2256, doi:10.1017/9781009157896.022.</ref>{{rp|2223}} This concept helps scientists understand the extent and magnitude of the [[effects of climate change]].

The Earth's surface warms as a direct consequence of increased atmospheric {{CO2}}, as well as increased concentrations of other [[Greenhouse gas|greenhouse gases]] such as [[nitrous oxide]] and [[methane]]. The increasing temperatures have secondary effects on the [[climate system]]. These secondary effects are called [[Climate change feedbacks|climate feedbacks]]. [[Positive feedback|Self-reinforcing feedbacks]] include for example the melting of [[Ice–albedo feedback|sunlight-reflecting ice]] as well as higher [[evapotranspiration]]. The latter effect increases average atmospheric water vapour, which is itself a [[greenhouse gas]].

Scientists do not know exactly how strong these climate feedbacks are. Therefore, it is difficult to predict the precise amount of warming that will result from a given increase in greenhouse gas concentrations. If climate sensitivity turns out to be on the high side of scientific estimates, the [[Paris Agreement]] goal of limiting [[global warming]] to below {{convert|2|C-change}} will be even more difficult to achieve.<ref name=":5" />

There are two main kinds of climate sensitivity: the ''transient climate response'' is the initial rise in global temperature when {{CO2}} levels double, and the ''equilibrium climate sensitivity'' is the larger long-term temperature increase after the planet adjusts to the doubling. Climate sensitivity is estimated by several methods: looking directly at [[Instrumental temperature record|temperature]] and greenhouse gas concentrations since the [[Industrial Revolution]] began around the 1750s, using [[proxy (climate)|indirect measurements]] from the Earth's distant past, and [[Climate model|simulating the climate]].

== Fundamentals ==
The rate at which energy reaches Earth (as sunlight) and leaves Earth (as heat radiation to space) [[radiation budget|must balance]], or the planet will get warmer or cooler. An imbalance between incoming and outgoing radiation energy is called [[radiative forcing]]. A warmer planet [[black-body radiation|radiates heat to space faster]] and so a new balance is eventually reached, with a higher temperature and [[ocean heat content|stored energy content]]. However, the warming of the planet also has [[climate feedbacks|knock-on effects]], which create further warming in an [[exacerbating feedback]] loop. Climate sensitivity is a measure of how much temperature change a given amount of radiative forcing will cause.<ref name=":7">{{cite journal |author=PALAEOSENS Project Members |date=November 2012 |title=Making sense of palaeoclimate sensitivity |url=http://academiccommons.columbia.edu/download/fedora_content/download/ac:162782/CONTENT/Paleosens_Project_Members_2012.pdf |url-status=live |journal=Nature |volume=491 |issue=7426 |pages=683–691 |bibcode=2012Natur.491..683P |doi=10.1038/nature11574 |pmid=23192145 |s2cid=2840337 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170815164923/https://academiccommons.columbia.edu/download/fedora_content/download/ac:162782/CONTENT/Paleosens_Project_Members_2012.pdf |archive-date=15 August 2017 |access-date=24 September 2013 |hdl=2078.1/118863}}</ref>  

=== Radiative forcing ===
{{Main|Radiative forcing|Earth's energy imbalance}}
Radiative forcings are generally quantified as [[Watt]]s per square meter (W/m<sup>2</sup>) and averaged over Earth's uppermost surface defined as the [[Tropopause|top of the atmosphere]].<ref name=IPCC1990/>  The magnitude of a forcing is specific to the physical driver and is defined ''relative to'' an accompanying time span of interest for its application.<ref>{{cite book |title=Radiative Forcing of Climate Change: Expanding the Concept and Addressing Uncertainties |author=National Research Council |publisher=The National Academic Press |year=2005 |doi=10.17226/11175|isbn=978-0-309-09506-8 }}</ref>  In the context of a contribution to long-term climate sensitivity from 1750 to 2020, the 50% increase in atmospheric {{chem|CO|2}} is characterized by a forcing of about +2.1&nbsp;W/m<sup>2</sup>.<ref>{{Cite web |url=https://www.esrl.noaa.gov/gmd/aggi/aggi.html |title=The NOAA Annual Greenhouse Gas Index (AGGI) |publisher=[[NOAA]] Global Monitoring Laboratory/Earth System Research Laboratories |author=Butler J. and Montzka S. |year=2020 }}</ref>   In the context of shorter-term contributions to Earth's energy imbalance (i.e. its heating/cooling rate), time intervals of interest may be as short as the interval between measurement or simulation data samplings, and are thus likely to be accompanied by smaller forcing values.  Forcings from such investigations have also been analyzed and reported at decadal time scales.<ref>{{cite web |url=https://phys.org/news/2021-03-humans-earth-energy.html |title=Direct observations confirm that humans are throwing Earth's energy budget off balance |website=phys.org |date=26 March 2021}}</ref><ref>{{cite journal |url=https://www.nature.com/articles/nature14240 |title=Observational determination of surface radiative forcing by {{chem|CO|2}} from 2000 to 2010 |author=Feldman, D.R., W.D. Collins, P.J. Gero, M.S. Torn, E.J. Mlawer, and T.R. Shippert |journal=Nature |volume=519 |date=2015-02-25 |issue=7543 |pages=339–343 |doi=10.1038/nature14240 |pmid=25731165 |bibcode=2015Natur.519..339F |s2cid=2137527 }}</ref>

Radiative forcing leads to long-term changes in global temperature.<ref name=MIT_explained>{{Cite web|url=https://news.mit.edu/2010/explained-radforce-0309|title=Explained: Radiative forcing|website=MIT News|date=10 March 2010 |access-date=2019-03-30|archive-date=25 August 2019|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190825003553/http://news.mit.edu/2010/explained-radforce-0309|url-status=live}}</ref> A number of factors contribute radiative forcing: increased [[downwelling]] radiation from the [[greenhouse effect]], variability in solar radiation from [[Milankovitch cycles|changes in planetary orbit]], changes in [[solar irradiance]], direct and indirect effects caused by aerosols (for example changes in [[albedo]] from cloud cover), and changes in land use (deforestation or the loss of reflective ice cover).<ref name=IPCC1990>''Climate Change: The IPCC Scientific Assessment'' (1990), Report prepared for Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change by Working Group I, Houghton JT, Jenkins GT, Ephraums JJ (eds.), [https://www.ipcc.ch/ipccreports/far/wg_I/ipcc_far_wg_I_chapter_02.pdf chapter 2, Radiative Forcing of Climate] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180808033533/http://www.ipcc.ch/ipccreports/far/wg_I/ipcc_far_wg_I_chapter_02.pdf|date=2018-08-08}}, pp. 41–68</ref> In contemporary research, radiative forcing by greenhouse gases is well understood. {{As of|2019|df=}}, large uncertainties remain for aerosols.<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Larson|first1=E. J. L.|last2=Portmann|first2=R. W.| name-list-style = vanc|date=2019-11-12|title=Anthropogenic aerosol drives uncertainty in future climate mitigation efforts|journal=Scientific Reports|language=en|volume=9|issue=1|page=16538|doi=10.1038/s41598-019-52901-3|doi-access=free|pmid=31719591|pmc=6851092|bibcode=2019NatSR...916538L|issn=2045-2322}}</ref><ref>Myhre, G., D. Shindell, F.-M. Bréon, W. Collins, J. Fuglestvedt, J. Huang, D. Koch, J.-F. Lamarque, D. Lee, B. Mendoza, T. Nakajima, A. Robock, G. Stephens, T. Takemura and H. Zhang, 2013: [https://archive.ipcc.ch/pdf/assessment-report/ar5/wg1/WG1AR5_Chapter08_FINAL.pdf Chapter 8: Anthropogenic and Natural Radiative Forcing]. Contribution of Working Group I to the Fifth Assessment Report of the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change] [Stocker, T.F., D. Qin, G.-K. Plattner, M. Tignor, S.K. Allen, J. Boschung, A. === Key numbers===
{{Further|Carbon dioxide in Earth's atmosphere|Instrumental temperature record}}
[[Carbon dioxide in Earth's atmosphere|Carbon dioxide]] ({{CO2}}) levels rose from 280 [[parts per million]] (ppm) in the 18th century, when humans in the [[Industrial Revolution]] started burning significant amounts of fossil fuel such as coal, to over 415 ppm by 2020. As {{CO2}} is a [[greenhouse gas]], it hinders heat energy from leaving the Earth's atmosphere. In 2016, atmospheric {{CO2}} levels had increased by 45% over preindustrial levels, and radiative forcing caused by increased {{CO2}} was already more than 50% higher than in pre-industrial times because of non-linear effects.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Myhre |first1=Gunnar |last2=Myhre |first2=Cathrine Lund |last3=Forster |first3=Piers M. |last4=Shine |first4=Keith P. |name-list-style=vanc |date=2017 |title=Halfway to doubling of CO2 radiative forcing |url=http://centaur.reading.ac.uk/72841/1/halfwayCO2doubling_revised_v2.pdf |journal=[[Nature Geoscience]] |volume=10 |issue=10 |pages=710–711 |doi=10.1038/ngeo3036 |bibcode=2017NatGe..10..710M |access-date=13 February 2020 |archive-date=26 April 2019 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190426231756/http://centaur.reading.ac.uk/72841/1/halfwayCO2doubling_revised_v2.pdf |url-status=live }}</ref><ref group="note">The {{CO2}} level in 2016 was 403 ppm, which is less than 50% higher than the pre-industrial {{CO2}} concentration of 278 ppm. However, because increased concentrations have a progressively-smaller warming effect, the Earth was already more than halfway to doubling of radiative forcing caused by {{CO2}}.</ref> Between the 18th-century start of the Industrial Revolution and the year 2020, the Earth's temperature rose by a little over one degree Celsius (about two degrees Fahrenheit).<ref>{{cite news|last=Watts|first=Jonathan|name-list-style=vanc|url=https://www.theguardian.com/environment/2018/oct/08/global-warming-must-not-exceed-15c-warns-landmark-un-report|title=We have 12 years to limit climate change catastrophe, warns UN|date=2018-10-08|work=[[The Guardian]]|access-date=2020-02-13|language=en-GB|issn=0261-3077|archive-date=11 August 2019|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190811175157/https://www.theguardian.com/environment/2018/oct/08/global-warming-must-not-exceed-15c-warns-landmark-un-report|url-status=live}}</ref>

=== Societal importance ===
Because the [[economics of climate change mitigation]] depend greatly on how quickly [[carbon neutrality]] needs to be achieved, climate sensitivity estimates can have important economic and policy-making implications. One study suggests that halving the uncertainty of the value for transient climate response (TCR) could save trillions of dollars.<ref name="Hope2015">{{cite journal | vauthors = Hope C | title = The $10 trillion value of better information about the transient climate response | journal = Philosophical Transactions. Series A, Mathematical, Physical, and Engineering Sciences | volume = 373 | issue = 2054 | article-number = 20140429 | date = November 2015 | pmid = 26438286 | doi = 10.1098/rsta.2014.0429 | bibcode = 2015RSPTA.37340429H | doi-access = free}}</ref> A higher climate sensitivity would mean more dramatic increases in temperature, which makes it more prudent to take significant climate action.<ref>{{cite journal | vauthors = Freeman MC, Wagner G, Zeckhauser RJ | title = Climate sensitivity uncertainty: when is good news bad? | journal = Philosophical Transactions. Series A, Mathematical, Physical, and Engineering Sciences | volume = 373 | issue = 2055 | article-number = 20150092 | date = November 2015 | pmid = 26460117 | doi = 10.1098/rsta.2015.0092 | bibcode = 2015RSPTA.37350092F | s2cid = 13843499 | url = http://eprints.whiterose.ac.uk/111971/1/For_repository.pdf | doi-access = free | access-date = 22 February 2020 | archive-date = 22 February 2020 | archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20200222153314/http://eprints.whiterose.ac.uk/111971/1/For_repository.pdf | url-status = live }}</ref> If climate sensitivity turns out to be on the high end of what scientists estimate, the [[Paris Agreement]] goal of limiting global warming to well below 2&nbsp;°C cannot be achieved, and temperature increases will exceed that limit, at least temporarily. One study estimated that emissions cannot be reduced fast enough to meet the 2&nbsp;°C goal if equilibrium climate sensitivity (the long-term measure) is higher than {{convert|3.4|C-change}}.<ref name=":5">{{Cite journal|last1=Tanaka|first1=Katsumasa|last2=O'Neill|first2=Brian C. | name-list-style = vanc |date=2018|title=The Paris Agreement zero-emissions goal is not always consistent with the 1.5&nbsp;°C and 2&nbsp;°C temperature targets |journal=Nature Climate Change|language=en|volume=8|issue=4|pages=319–324|doi=10.1038/s41558-018-0097-x|bibcode=2018NatCC...8..319T|s2cid=91163896|issn=1758-6798}}</ref> The more sensitive the climate system is to changes in greenhouse gas concentrations, the more likely it is to have decades when temperatures are much higher or much lower than the longer-term average.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.independent.co.uk/voices/europe-heatwave-climate-change-europe-global-warming-science-a9018426.html|title=Opinion: Europe is burning just as scientists offer a chilling truth about climate change|last=Dyke|first=James|date=2019-07-24|website=The Independent|language=en|access-date=2019-07-26|name-list-style=vanc|archive-date=25 July 2019|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190725181005/https://www.independent.co.uk/voices/europe-heatwave-climate-change-europe-global-warming-science-a9018426.html|url-status=live}}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Nijsse|first1=Femke J. M. M.|last2=Cox|first2=Peter M.|last3=Huntingford|first3=Chris|last4=Williamson|first4=Mark S.|date=2019|title=Decadal global temperature variability increases strongly with climate sensitivity|url=http://nora.nerc.ac.uk/id/eprint/524582/1/N524582PP.pdf|journal=Nature Climate Change|language=en|volume=9|issue=8|pages=598–601|bibcode=2019NatCC...9..598N|doi=10.1038/s41558-019-0527-4|s2cid=198914522|issn=1758-6798|name-list-style=vanc|access-date=8 March 2020|archive-date=6 May 2020|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200506162654/http://nora.nerc.ac.uk/id/eprint/524582/1/N524582PP.pdf|url-status=live}}</ref>

== Factors that determine sensitivity ==
The radiative forcing caused by a doubling of atmospheric {{CO2}} levels (from the pre-industrial 280 ppm) is approximately 3.7 [[watt]]s per square meter (W/m<sup>2</sup>). In the absence of feedbacks, the energy imbalance would eventually result in roughly {{convert|1|C-change}} of [[global warming]]. That figure is straightforward to calculate by using the [[Stefan–Boltzmann law]]<ref group="note">The calculation is as follows. In equilibrium, the energy of incoming and outgoing radiation have to balance. The outgoing radiation <math>F</math> is given by the [[Stefan–Boltzmann law]]: <math>F = -\sigma T^4</math>. When incoming radiation increases, the outgoing radiation and therefore temperature must increase as well. The temperature rise <math> \Delta T_{2 \times CO_2}</math> ''directly caused'' by the additional radiative forcing, <math>\Delta F_{2 \times CO_2}</math> because of the doubling of {{CO2}} is then given by

:<math>\Delta F_{2 \times CO_2} = \frac{dF}{dT} \Delta T_{2 \times CO_2}  = 4 \sigma T^3 \Delta T_{2 \times CO_2}</math>.
Given an [[effective temperature]] of {{convert|255|K|C F}}, a constant [[lapse rate]], the value of the [[Stefan–Boltzmann constant]] <math>\sigma</math> of 5.67 <math> \times 10^{-8}</math>W/m<sup>2</sup> K<sup>−4</sup> and <math>\Delta F_{2\times CO_2}</math>around 4 W/m<sup>2</sup>, the equation gives a climate sensitivity of a world without feedback of approximately 1 K.</ref><ref name=":6">{{Cite journal|last=Roe|first=Gerard|s2cid=66109238| name-list-style = vanc|date=2009|title=Feedbacks, Timescales, and Seeing Red|journal=Annual Review of Earth and Planetary Sciences|volume=37|issue=1|pages=93–115|doi=10.1146/annurev.earth.061008.134734|bibcode=2009AREPS..37...93R}}</ref> and is undisputed.<ref name="rahmstorf2008">{{Cite book |last=Rahmstorf |first=Stefan |author-link=Stefan Rahmstorf |title=Global Warming: Looking Beyond Kyoto |publisher=Brookings Institution Press |year=2008 |editor-last=Zedillo |editor-first=Ernesto |pages=34–53 |chapter=Anthropogenic Climate Change: Revisiting the Facts |access-date=14 August 2008 |chapter-url=http://www.pik-potsdam.de/~stefan/Publications/Book_chapters/Rahmstorf_Zedillo_2008.pdf |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190714024054/http://www.pik-potsdam.de/~stefan/Publications/Book_chapters/Rahmstorf_Zedillo_2008.pdf |archive-date=14 July 2019 |url-status=live |name-list-style=vanc}}</ref>

A further contribution arises from [[climate change feedback|climate feedbacks]], both [[exacerbating feedback|self-reinforcing]] and [[suppressing feedback|balancing]].<ref>{{cite journal | vauthors = Lenton TM, Rockström J, Gaffney O, Rahmstorf S, Richardson K, Steffen W, Schellnhuber HJ | title = Climate tipping points - too risky to bet against | journal = Nature | volume = 575 | issue = 7784 | pages = 592–595 | date = November 2019 | pmid = 31776487 | doi = 10.1038/d41586-019-03595-0 | bibcode = 2019Natur.575..592L | doi-access = free | hdl = 10871/40141 | hdl-access = free }}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Armstrong McKay |first1=David I. |last2=Staal |first2=Arie |last3=Abrams |first3=Jesse F. |last4=Winkelmann |first4=Ricarda |last5=Sakschewski |first5=Boris |last6=Loriani |first6=Sina |last7=Fetzer |first7=Ingo |last8=Cornell |first8=Sarah E. |last9=Rockström |first9=Johan |last10=Lenton |first10=Timothy M. |date=2022-09-09 |title=Exceeding 1.5°C global warming could trigger multiple climate tipping points |url=https://www.science.org/doi/10.1126/science.abn7950 |journal=Science |language=en |volume=377 |issue=6611 |article-number=eabn7950 |doi=10.1126/science.abn7950 |pmid=36074831 |hdl=10871/131584 |s2cid=252161375 |issn=0036-8075|hdl-access=free |url-access=subscription }}</ref> The uncertainty in climate sensitivity estimates is mostly from the feedbacks in the climate system, including [[Water vapor feedback#Role of water vapor|water vapour feedback]], [[ice–albedo feedback]], [[cloud feedback]], and [[lapse rate]] feedback.<ref name="rahmstorf2008" />  Balancing feedbacks tend to counteract warming by increasing the rate at which energy is radiated to space from a warmer planet. Self-reinfocing feedbacks increase warming; for example, higher temperatures can cause ice to melt, which reduces the ice area and the amount of sunlight the ice reflects, which in turn results in less heat energy being radiated back into space. The reflectiveness of a surface is called [[albedo]]. Climate sensitivity depends on the balance between those feedbacks.<ref name=":6" />
